all_scored.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
all_scored.summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

all_scored.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
all_scored.summary: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.

all_scored.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
all_scored.summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.

all_scored.title: Implementation and Software-in-the-Loop Evaluation of a Trans-Domain Digital Twin Architecture for Autonomous Guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV Without Online GNSS
all_scored.summary: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or unreliable in enclosed spaces, blind spots caused by natural obstacles and structures, and environments affected by radio interference and signal spoofing during electronic warfare. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a system based on a Trans-Domain Digital Twin (TDDT) for autonomous guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV. Independent navigation, flight dynamics, and meteorological models are coordinated within a cycle of state estimation, prediction, decision-making, command execution, and feedback. Data from inertial, magnetic, pressure, and airspeed sensors, together with environmental information, form the basis for estimation and prediction. Furthermore, a shared state, temporal synchronization, preservation of information provenance, and command traceability establish continuity between models and decisions. The system was tested with a simulated physical twin in a software-in-the-loop environment. Vertical takeoff, movement toward the destination, landing, and autonomous stopping were recorded, and the dynamic model was adjusted to a limited extent based on sensor-derived feedback. Separating the evaluation reference from navigation inputs enabled independent assessment of positioning error and computational performance. The results confirm operational coordination, decision traceability, and closed-loop guidance under the tested conditions, providing a reproducible platform for the development and evaluation of navigation without satellite-based positioning.

all_scored.title: Group-Balanced Supervised Fine-Tuning for Knowledge-Intensive Domains
all_scored.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) weights every supervised token equally, so on knowledge-dense corpora the loss budget follows token count rather than importance: on a legal QA benchmark, citation strings absorb 81% of the supervised loss weight budget while the answers being taught absorb 5%. We present Group-Balanced SFT (GB-SFT), which equalizes the loss budget across the semantic roles of tokens within a target sequence. With one tunable dial and one structural switch, GB-SFT contains standard SFT, class- and span-level balancing as corners whose geometry we characterize exactly. On benchmarks in law, medicine, code, and mathematics, we show across model families that: (i) GB- SFT injects new knowledge better than uniform SFT, pointwise token weighting, memory editing, and matched-budget data mixing; (ii) it matches the injection of masking out everything but the knowledge payload while retaining the citation recall that masking destroys (0.98 vs. 0.38); and (iii) role-aware grouping carries the gain: label-free partitions recover at most a third of it, an LLM tagger nearly all where the groups are lexically distinctive; and and (iv) the budget governs what fine-tuning breaks as well as what it learns, acting as a monotone lever on the safety-guardrail erosion SFT causes, at matched task accuracy. We release two new contamination-controlled knowledge-injection benchmarks with validated ground truth.

all_scored.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
all_scored.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

all_scored.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
all_scored.summary: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.

all_scored.title: When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection
all_scored.summary: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.

all_scored.title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
all_scored.summary: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

all_scored.title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions
all_scored.summary: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.

all_scored.title: Evaluable Language-Model Treatment Policies for Sepsis Resuscitation via Offline Value-Guided Selection
all_scored.summary: Offline treatment learning must balance imitation, which stays close to logged evidence but ignores outcomes, against value maximisation, which uses outcomes but drifts toward treatments the records cannot verify. Numerical reinforcement learning strikes this balance during training. For large language models (LLMs), directly using sparse retrospective outcomes for fine-tuning raises challenges of delayed credit assignment and limited evidence for alternative treatments. We present R-LLMC, which strikes the balance at inference for sepsis resuscitation. A behaviour-supervised LLM, decoded into an exact distribution over 25 vasopressor-fluid actions, proposes clinician-anchored candidates; an offline critic selects among them by estimated long-term value. The policy has a closed form for off-policy evaluation, and its rationale is written after selection, so explanation cannot steer treatment. In experiments on held-out MIMIC-III patients, R-LLMC exceeded the clinician reference in doubly robust value by +0.214 (95\% CI 0.091-0.300), with fitted Q evaluation agreeing.
