The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

all_scored.title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
all_scored.summary: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.

all_scored.title: SurgeCount: A Protocol-Guided Composition Harness for Bimanual Surgical Sponge Counting
all_scored.summary: We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.

all_scored.title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
all_scored.summary: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

all_scored.title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
all_scored.summary: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

all_scored.title: Predicting Rare-Mode Collapse in Recursive Generative Training from Single-Generation Calibration
all_scored.summary: Recursive generative training can preserve sample counts in a rare region while silently eroding its characteristic core. Mapping this finite-horizon collapse across real-data quotas, rare prevalences, and feedback perturbations via exhaustive multi-generation chains is computationally prohibitive. We develop a decoupled framework that forecasts multi-generation collapse probabilities and locates operating risk boundaries from independent single-generation conditional fits alone. Pairing an exact three-source multinomial count law with single-generation response banks propagates count marginals in closed form, backed by explicit calibration-error and boundary-resolution bounds. For additive Gaussian perturbations, we further prove that equal-variance all-row and sparse policies reverse their boundary-crossing order at a unique hyperplane distance. Across a 2,178-setting count benchmark, exact propagation cuts risk mean absolute error (MAE) from 1.85 to 0.49 percentage points (pp). Across ten two-dimensional learners, calibration achieves 2.60--5.69~pp six-round core MAE on nine stationary learners (65--81\% below an unperturbed baseline), diagnoses non-stationary outlier drift in standard DDIM (16.38~pp) via a stability probe, and resolves the predicted six-round geometric reversal. On Fashion-MNIST latent flow-matching chains, calibration outperforms direct-chain Gaussian-process interpolation at lower fit budgets and tracks the 20\% latent-perturbation boundary shift (3.14 versus 10.78~pp MAE for proportion copying) driven by opposing inflow to the rare region and outflow from its core.

all_scored.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
all_scored.summary: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

all_scored.title: MUNDO: a multiresolution generative framework for temporal downscaling
all_scored.summary: Dynamical systems are often observed at coarse temporal resolution through sparse states or temporal aggregates, leaving the underlying fine-scale trajectories unresolved. Recovering these trajectories requires probabilistic models that capture the unresolved variability while remaining consistent with the observations. We present MUNDO (Multiresolution UNified DOwnscaling), a generative framework for temporal downscaling under general linear observation operators. MUNDO introduces a null-space parameterization that enforces exact observation consistency in a single network evaluation, unifying temporal interpolation and disaggregation. To capture complex multiscale dynamics, we leverage reverse Markov learning to factorize the observation operator into a hierarchy of successive coarsenings. Each level models only the degrees of freedom lost between adjacent resolutions. We evaluate MUNDO on two-scale Lorenz-96, four two-dimensional physical systems, and multivariate ERA5 reanalysis over Europe, for both temporal interpolation and disaggregation. Across datasets and tasks, MUNDO generally outperforms flow-based baselines. Single-step MUNDO achieves strong predictive skill, while recursive MUNDO generally improves temporal realism and ensemble calibration, with better spread-skill agreement and predictive coverage.

all_scored.title: Potential Games for Self-Neighborhood Channel Mixing in Graph Neural Networks
all_scored.summary: Graph message passing must balance two competing objectives: incorporating neighborhood signals while preserving node-specific information. We model this trade-off as a game in which nodes choose how to mix their own representations with strict-neighborhood aggregates. For fixed channel representations, task supervision defines a common-payoff game, while local distinctness payoffs induce an exact potential game whose potential is the degree-normalized strict Dirichlet energy. We introduce CG2, which amortizes these choices through a shared six-parameter policy per layer based on local channel statistics and can be trained using either objective. Controlled comparisons show that the shared task-trained policy improves mean performance over fixed mixing on three of five heterophily benchmarks, with significant gains on two, while free per-node actions trained with either objective rarely improve on the same baseline. On the ECHO long-range benchmark, the clearest contribution of the gate appears on eccentricity, where the task-trained policy substantially reduces prediction error.

all_scored.title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference
all_scored.summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.

all_scored.title: SchemaCaps: When a Compatible Tool Update Silently Widens an AI Agent's Authority
all_scored.summary: The tools users approve for their AI agents keep changing their JSON input schemas. Of 8 surveyed MCP clients and scanners, none is observed or documented to re-approve a tool whose input schema widens (two not determinable). We define non-amplification over the coordinates visible in the schema (declared arguments and undeclared fields, on effective values) and a re-binding rule decided by subschema inclusion, trusting no field labels by default and conservative up to its checker and tested case analysis. Evidence: a Coq proof of composition; 48 regression tests; an exact-reference benchmark, where the reviewed version of the rule silently re-bound 27 amplifying changes, now fixed; and a pilot on 604 releases of 39 public MCP servers. There, 412 of 580 compatible schema changes widen some coordinate, yet compatibility re-binds them silently. The authors' adjudicated double annotation finds at least 76 that add or widen an authority-bearing argument (66 of the 84 a name-based labeller flags, plus 10 it misses). On existing tools, the rule asks 645 re-approvals, against 1,197 for pinning the input schema (2,004 with descriptions) and 617 for compatibility. Behaviour change behind an identical schema remains out of reach.

all_scored.title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments
all_scored.summary: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.

all_scored.title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation
all_scored.summary: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.

all_scored.title: MTL-MHOL: Predicting Online Conversions under Delayed Feedback and Data Sparsity
all_scored.summary: This paper proposes the model-agnostic Multi-Task Learning Multi-Head Online Learning (MTL-MHOL) framework for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. Existing approaches typically address key challenges in CVR prediction, such as delayed feedback and data sparsity, in isolation or lack flexibility and practical applicability. MTL-MHOL adopts a time bucketing approach to account for delayed feedback and combines it with multi-task learning of an auxiliary task to mitigate data sparsity. We evaluate the framework on proprietary datasets from a private company and on a public dataset from Criteo. MTL-MHOL matches or outperforms all benchmark models in terms of Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) and Relative Cross Entropy (RCE), and it correctly captures temporal trends in the data using an MLP backbone, while maintaining strong performance with a DeepFM backbone. In particular, MTL-MHOL matches the performance of the advanced delayed-feedback method FSIW, outperforms the entire-space approach ESMM by 21.5% in RCE, and achieves up to 81% lift in RCE compared to the best-performing classical benchmark.

all_scored.title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
all_scored.summary: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer

all_scored.title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
all_scored.summary: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

all_scored.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
all_scored.summary: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

all_scored.title: JONES-19: A Cultural Image Dataset Based on The Grammar of Ornament
all_scored.summary: We introduce JONES-19, a high-quality image dataset documenting 1,901 ornament designs belonging to nineteen human cultures. The images and their annotations are based on an open access archive of The Grammar of Ornament (London, 1856), by Owen Jones. The dataset poses numerous challenges as a benchmark for computer vision classification tasks and for research at the intersection of machine learning and art and design: a small sample size, image samples of human-designed artifacts rather than common objects in-context or natural scenes, imbalanced class distribution, and image distinctions based on fine details involving line patterns, reliefs, and colors. As a design-inspired dataset, JONES-19 can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, such as visual recognition, data-efficient learning, art-historical research, architectural style analysis, and cultural heritage. This paper describes the curation of the JONES-19 dataset and reports a baseline classification benchmark that evaluates the suitability of the dataset for training classifiers and exposes insights into inter-class relationships--particularly cultural similarities--by examining patterns in misclassification errors. The dataset and its accompanying documentation are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/harvardseas-cultural-ornaments/JONES-19.

all_scored.title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
all_scored.summary: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

all_scored.title: BEND: Spectral Bregman Losses for Multi-Image Unlearning in Diffusion Models
all_scored.summary: Diffusion models memorize training images and reproduce them almost verbatim when prompted, creating copyright and privacy liabilities. Data unlearning erases the influence of specific training samples from a trained model without retraining, and is two-sided: it must forget the targets while preserving generation quality on everything else. Prior methods use the squared-L2 diffusion loss, at most with a hand-set frequency mask; however, it is known that every Bregman divergence is a mathematically valid choice and the squared-L2 is only the simplest example. BEND is the first to search this family: it fits a spectral Bregman divergence to the unlearning task through a bilevel loop, so the loss itself is shaped to forget thoroughly while protecting quality. It also redirects a memorized image to the mean of its retain images, where ReTrack, the state of the art, redirects it to a single near-copy. On Stable Diffusion, a single BEND model erases all 48 verifiably memorized benchmark images at once. It forgets at least as much as per-target, sequential, and jointly trained ReTrack (SSCD 0.084 versus 0.094-0.120), at the quality of the model before unlearning (CLIP-IQA 0.81 versus 0.64-0.69). BEND also outperforms the state of the art on CelebA-HQ in all three measures of the benchmark, and matches or exceeds it on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

all_scored.title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
all_scored.summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.

all_scored.title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation
all_scored.summary: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

all_scored.title: HWRE-Bench: Can LLM Agents Understand Hardware They Did Not Design?
all_scored.summary: Hardware benchmarks for LLM agents all run the design flow forward, from a specification to RTL, a layout or a bug fix. We ask the reverse question: given an implemented artifact, such as a layout, a gate-level netlist or a protected simulation model, can an agent work out what it does well enough to act on that knowledge? We introduce HWRE-Bench, a benchmark for agentic hardware reverse engineering built on one observation. Each step of the forward flow discards information (names, hierarchy, word-level structure, generator parameters, the programming model), and a reverse-engineering task asks the agent to recover what was lost and to prove it with an executable deliverable that the artifact alone cannot supply. Since layout extraction is now mechanical and a correct netlist is already a cycle-exact model, every task carries a mandatory copy-the-netlist control that must score zero. HWRE-Bench spans five tracks (Extract, Abstract, Audit, Interoperate, Modify), four information-loss levels and white- versus black-box access, all on original designs. We report a pilot of 148 rollouts from two agents on four seed tasks under 16 conditions, with stage-annotated trajectories. Agents built their own layout extractors and audited a sanitized layout as reliably as a netlist, at about 27% more turns. Keyless, equivalence-preserving obfuscation changed neither pass rates nor defect-repair scores. Whether agents read the structure at all depended on task framing rather than on necessity, so pass rate alone does not show understanding. Provider safety filters stopped 16% of one agent's runs on the audit tasks. These results argue for deliverables beyond equivalence and for reporting run validity explicitly.

all_scored.title: Time Series Foundation Models on the Edge
all_scored.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast zero-shot with accuracy exceeding that of task-specific models, and the smaller ones fit on edge devices. Operational deployments must refresh their forecast as new observations arrive, and privacy and latency requirements often force this refresh onto resource-constrained edge devices. To serve as a forecasting system there, a TSFM must refresh quickly, keep latency and peak memory bounded as the stream grows, and retain its accuracy as the observed history accumulates. Refreshing incrementally without altering the forecast requires temporal causality: non-causal models recompute at every update, causal attention admits a KV cache that grows linearly, and causal recurrent models update a fixed-size state in constant time and memory. We make these states persist across refreshes for every causal architecture and verify equivalence to full recomputation. We evaluate nine TSFM configurations on univariate forecasting against all three requirements, measuring accuracy as a function of context length, single-refresh latency, and latency and memory on streams of up to one million time steps on a server-grade GPU and three edge devices. No model gains on average accuracy beyond its trained context and most lose it well before the full history is reached, while KV caches leave latency and memory growing linearly with the retained history. TiRex-2 is the only one of the nine configurations meeting all three requirements: it refreshes in 14 ms on the GPU and 120 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5, keeps latency, energy and peak memory constant over a million steps, and retains its accuracy on the untruncated history.

all_scored.title: Low-Rank Tensor Representations for Efficient Multimarginal Optimal Transport
all_scored.summary: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce Low-Rank Multimarginal Optimal Transport (LRMOT), which restricts transport plans to tensors with bounded multilinear rank, providing a compact and structured representation of multimarginal couplings. This structure enables efficient algorithms with a low memory footprint. We establish approximation bounds for the resulting low-rank formulations and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed algorithms substantially reduce computational time while achieving solutions with low transport cost.

all_scored.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
all_scored.summary: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. LeanReviewBench provides a testbed for reviewing semantic correspondence in existing mathematical formalization projects. LeanReviewBench is available at https://github.com/MechMath/LeanReviewBench.

all_scored.title: AutoClip-DPZO: Practical Private Clipping Selection for Differentially Private Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
all_scored.summary: Differentially private zeroth-order optimization (DPZO) is a promising approach for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning, offering exceptional memory efficiency. However, its utility is highly sensitive to the clipping threshold $C$, a key DP-specific hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between noise injection and clipping bias. Existing DPZO methods typically tune $C$ by repeatedly evaluating candidate values and reporting the best result, which is computationally expensive and incurs additional privacy cost that must be accounted for under DP. Designing a practical DP procedure for selecting $C$ in DPZO is challenging because no fixed choice performs well across settings, straightforward search-based strategies suffer from poor utility and efficiency, and existing clipping-selection methods for DPSGD do not transfer well to DPZO due to its fundamentally different error regime. In this paper, we propose AutoClip-DPZO, a practical DP method that automatically and efficiently selects $C$ for DPZO. Our key idea is to avoid fine-tuning-based search by reducing clipping selection to a private quantile estimation problem, where the target quantile depends only on public privacy and training parameters. To derive this selection rule, we develop a novel characterization of DPZO error as a function of $C$ that captures both noise variance and clipping bias while remaining accurate and easy to optimize. Experiments show that AutoClip-DPZO achieves utility comparable to that obtained with the optimal $C$, while avoiding repeated fine-tuning-based search and incurring negligible additional overhead. Moreover, AutoClip-DPZO does not rely on sensitive hyperparameters.

all_scored.title: FMSNO: Scaling Surface Neural Operators by Learned Flow Matching Reparametrisation
all_scored.summary: We propose the Flow Matching Surface Neural Operator (FMSNO), which combines learning a shared map from irregular surface meshes to a regular two-dimensional grid on the sphere and training a neural operator on the regular grid. Constructing a separate map for each new geometry can dominate inference time on large meshes. We initially pretrain the mapping by flow matching using precomputed optimal transport maps as targets and then continue its training using combined geometry and CFD objectives. We apply it to unseen geometries in a single forward pass. The learned flow deforms the surface points, and we project its endpoints onto the sphere. We then splat geometric features onto the spherical grid, apply a neural operator (we tested both Fourier and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and interpolate its output back to the surface. For a mesh with $N$ points, evaluating the map costs O(N), and the full prediction costs O(NlogN) with the FNO backbone. We evaluate surface pressure prediction on ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, and drag coefficient prediction on DrivAerNet++. Across the three pressure benchmarks, our accuracy is on par with that of the most accurate baseline. On a surface with one million points, our method achieves a 354x end-to-end inference speedup over that baseline while keeping the same memory usage asymptotics of O(N).

all_scored.title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction
all_scored.summary: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.

all_scored.title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
all_scored.summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

all_scored.title: Operator-Valued Q-Learning: Compositional Bellman Recursions for Order-Sensitive Decision Making
all_scored.summary: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.

all_scored.title: Voyag: Joint Multi-Intent Detection and Execution-Relation Classification for In-Vehicle Voice Assistants
all_scored.summary: An in-vehicle voice assistant must decide not only which intents an utterance contains but also how co-active intents may be executed: concurrently, in a fixed order, or not at all without arbitration. We present Voyag, a single-forward decision model that jointly predicts ten controlled vehicle-intent slots and a three-way execution relation (parallel, sequential, mutually exclusive) over each co-active intent pair. Voyag combines a multilingual ModernBERT-style encoder (mmBERT-base, 306.9M parameters), a typed per-slot choice head, and a lightweight GroupCalibration relation head (1.61M parameters) that consumes marker hidden states, pooled context, explicit resource-requirement profiles, and symmetrized outer-product conflict features. All objectives are optimized in one joint loss: soft cross-entropy over slot choices, focal cross-entropy over relations, and a mutex-consistency penalty. On a synthetic Chinese vehicle-life benchmark with semantic scene-level splits and a leakage audit (30,017 / 3,473 / 5,000 groups), validation-only selection yields 0.9893 slot accuracy and 0.0526 expected calibration error over 50,000 slot decisions. Conditioned on gold intents, the relation head reaches 0.8548 accuracy, 0.8473 macro-F1, and 0.6062 mutually-exclusive recall over 4,000 pairs; end to end with one encoder forward it reaches 0.8530 accuracy and 0.8464 macro-F1. Against a two-stage rule pipeline, the aggregate end-to-end gain is small and borderline, so we claim no aggregate advantage; the learned head's advantage lies in sequential and parallel recall where surface rules are blind. We report rule baselines with a tautology disclosure and a held-out thermal conflict failure.

all_scored.title: StutterStigma-TR: A Novel Turkish Dataset and Target-Aware BERT Framework for Stuttering-Related Stigma Detection
all_scored.summary: Computational research on disability-related ableist harm remains limited, and condition specific resources for stuttering-related stigma are particularly scarce. This study introduces StutterStigma-TR, a Turkish dataset of 6,019 public X/Twitter posts annotated as Stigmatizing, Non-stigmatizing/contextual, or Supportive using a speech and language therapy-informed protocol with independent lived-experience evaluation. We also propose StutterStigma-BERT, a BERTurk-based target-aware framework that combines explicit target marking, target-span representation, target-conditioned context, character-level and handcrafted orthographic information, and gated discourse cues. The framework is evaluated in complementary three-class and binary settings using controlled three-seed ablation analyses and final 20-seed robustness evaluations. Under the common training protocol, Gated Discourse-OrthoTarget trained with cross-entropy is selected as the final configuration for both tasks based on internal-validation Macro-F1. Across 20 random seeds, the final three-class model achieves a mean Macro-F1 of 73.54%, while the final binary model achieves 85.17% using validation-selected decision thresholds. Task adapted harmful-language comparators are additionally evaluated under the common training protocol, and the proposed model obtains the highest mean Macro-F1 among them. For the primary three-class task, matched backbone analyses show higher internal validation Macro-F1 with BERTurk than with TurkishBERTweet or Turkish Mamba, while substantial train-validation separation persists across all three backbones. Separate direct-transfer and zero-shot experiments examine performance without StutterStigma-TR supervision. Across the task-adapted, direct-transfer, and zero-shot comparisons, the condition-specific supervised systems retain the strongest aggregate performance.

all_scored.title: TriSegAgent: Context-Efficient 3D Annotation with MLLMs via Tri-Planes
all_scored.summary: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.

all_scored.title: OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
all_scored.summary: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.

all_scored.title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
all_scored.summary: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.

all_scored.title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
all_scored.summary: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

all_scored.title: Separating Protocol Effects from Spatio-Temporal Evidence in Person Re-Identification Re-Ranking
all_scored.summary: Spatio-temporal priors re-rank person re-identification matches using the camera pair and the time gap, and are reported to add large gains on Market-1501. We ask how much of such a gain encodes the evaluation protocol rather than learned spatio-temporal evidence. Starting from a course-project re-ranker that adds log camera-transition and log time-gap terms to cosine similarity, we train a strong ResNet-50 baseline (Rank-1 94.3 %, mAP 86.2 % over three seeds), choose the fusion weights on an identity-disjoint validation split and evaluate on the official test set with control priors. The repository form adds 2.30 mAP points, but a one-parameter penalty on same-camera pairs alone adds 2.19: the protocol never places a true match in the query's camera, so the penalty removes distractors for free. The time term of that form is almost unused; a pair-level diagnostic traces this to its modelling the time gap given a match without dividing by the gap distribution of all candidate pairs. A likelihood-ratio prior adds 4.04 points without the penalty and 5.62 with it; shuffling the time stamps removes the extra gain, so about 3.43 points are tied to identity. The prior fixes the first-ranked match of 4.2 % of the queries and breaks it for 0.1 %. The gain shrinks as the visual baseline improves (11.9 to 5.62 points between a 70.5 % and a 86.2 % mAP model) and concentrates on queries whose true matches share the query's video sequence. The study covers one dataset, one backbone and three seeds.

all_scored.title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling
all_scored.summary: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.

all_scored.title: Small data machine learning: the trilemma of low-sample tabular regimes
all_scored.summary: Small tabular datasets leave few observations for choosing a model and assessing its predictions. We examine these competing demands in controlled simulations and on six public datasets, using SmallGBM and SmallMLP as fixed-configuration case studies. Three results illustrate why the choice of evaluation matters. First, at n = 100, five-fold cross-validation overstated the gain from tuning XGBoost by 0.063 ROC-AUC on random labels, while tuning improved independent-test ROC-AUC by 0.0078 on a Gaussian mixture. Second, when 20% of binary training labels were flipped, the median within-trial ROC-AUC loss was 0.0210 for SmallGBM and 0.0778 for a fixed 200-tree XGBoost configuration. A separate regression experiment showed the sensitivity of squared-error training to heavy-tailed responses. Third, in a heteroscedastic regression experiment, locally weighted SmallMLP intervals covered about one percentage point more test responses than ordinary split conformal intervals at both tested dimensions. Their mean widths also increased. On a Gaussian classification task with linear log odds, logistic regression achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC at all seven training sizes. These experiments identify settings in which a small-data model helps and quantify the cost of its assumptions.

all_scored.title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
all_scored.summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

all_scored.title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
all_scored.summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

all_scored.title: STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience
all_scored.summary: A tool router retrieves a few candidate tools per request and lets a language model choose. Methods that share experience across organizations add past requests about each tool to what the router retrieves. StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/<org>/STUN-Bench.

all_scored.title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
all_scored.summary: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

all_scored.title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration
all_scored.summary: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.

all_scored.title: UnderGrasp: Envelopment-Oriented Grasp Refinement for an Underactuated Gripper
all_scored.summary: Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance, while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators do not fully capture the approach-closure process. Conventional collision filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable contact. We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors from a frozen generator. The model jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR) and the envelopment rate (ER) among successful grasps from 0.55/0.12 to 0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from 0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52, supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36 to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable execution under contact. Project page: https://dishenliu2004-hub.github.io/undergrasp-site/

all_scored.title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
all_scored.summary: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

all_scored.title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
all_scored.summary: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

all_scored.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
all_scored.summary: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page.
